overview: Republicans in the House used a procedural vote on Tuesday to stop an attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a reprieve that may last only until Democrats take over Congress in January. Both parties are choosing leaders after the midterms: House Republicans elected Jim Jordan to lead them in the minority, Senate Republicans re-elected John Thune, and Sen. Bernie Sanders said he would not support Chuck Schumer as the Democrats' Senate leader. Consumer prices rose more than expected in October, pulling stocks lower and strengthening expectations of a Federal Reserve rate increase in December. Overseas, Russian and Ukrainian officials met for U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi, and British police arrested a U.S. soldier on suspicion of spying for Russia.

stories.headline: House Republicans block Massie's bid to impeach Defense Secretary Hegseth
stories.summary: The House voted 211-204 on Tuesday to send Rep. Thomas Massie's impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, which halts the effort for now. President Trump welcomed the result. Democrats, who take control of Congress in January, could bring impeachment up again.
stories.why_it_matters: The articles concern how the US entered and is fighting the war with Iran and other military strikes, so the vote is a test of whether Congress will check the Pentagon's use of force. With Democrats taking both chambers in January, the question of Hegseth's future is likely to return.
stories.background: Pete Hegseth has led the Pentagon since 2025, and the US has been at war with Iran in 2026. Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who lost a Trump-backed primary this year and is retiring, first moved to impeach Hegseth in September. His eight articles accuse Hegseth of starting the Iran war illegally, directing extrajudicial killings and ignoring rules meant to limit civilian deaths. Because the resolution was privileged, the House had to act on it, and Republican leaders chose a procedural vote rather than an up-or-down impeachment vote. Democrats won both chambers in last week's midterm elections and take over in January.

facts.text: The House voted 211-204 on Tuesday to send the impeachment resolution to the Judiciary Committee, which halts the immediate drive but does not stop Democrats from reviving it after January.
Every House Republican except Massie voted to spare Hegseth, CBS News reported.
NPR reported the House had been on course for a floor vote on impeachment Wednesday before Republicans used the procedural vote.
Trump welcomed the outcome and called Hegseth a 'Great American Patriot'.
Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) said she and other lawmakers could not reach the Capitol in time to vote because of a traffic incident and a police escort.
The eight articles accuse Hegseth of illegally starting the war with Iran, directing extrajudicial killings and ignoring laws meant to minimize civilian casualties.
At his first news conference in six months, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a 'farce' and a 'stunt' and said it was about 'policy disagreements'.
A former Hegseth spokesman called on him to resign and said he should be impeached, CNN reported.
Massie first moved to impeach Hegseth over the Iran war in September.

stories.headline: Republicans pick Jim Jordan to lead House GOP and keep John Thune in the Senate
stories.summary: House Republicans on Tuesday chose Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio over Rep. Steve Scalise to lead them as the minority party in the next Congress. Senate Republicans re-elected John Thune as their leader after rejecting a push by some senators to delay the vote. Both parties are reorganizing after Republicans lost control of both chambers in the midterms.
stories.why_it_matters: These leaders will decide how Republicans respond to a Democratic Congress during the last two years of Trump's term, including on spending deals, investigations and any impeachment efforts.
stories.background: Republicans lost both the House and the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, and will be in the minority when the new Congress starts in January. House Speaker Mike Johnson said the day after the election that he would not run for minority leader. Jim Jordan, chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, co-founded the hardline Freedom Caucus and is a close Trump ally; he had sought to lead House Republicans twice before. John Thune of South Dakota has led Senate Republicans for the past two years.

stories.headline: Bernie Sanders says he won't back Chuck Schumer as Senate Democratic leader
stories.summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he will not support Chuck Schumer to lead Senate Democrats in the new Congress, saying 'the time is now for change.' No one has formally challenged Schumer, though Sen. Chris Van Hollen is considering it. Schumer said he is confident he will become majority leader.
stories.why_it_matters: Whoever leads the new Democratic Senate majority will set its agenda on spending, investigations and Trump's nominees for the next two years.
stories.background: Democrats won control of the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms, with at least 54 seats according to The Guardian. Chuck Schumer of New York is the current Democratic leader and is seeking to become majority leader. Some progressives, a major union and some newly elected senators want new leadership. Sanders, an independent from Vermont, caucuses with the Democrats and is a leading progressive.

stories.headline: House Oversight report says federal government failed Epstein's victims for decades
stories.summary: The Republican-led House Oversight Committee released a 137-page final report on its 15-month Epstein investigation, faulting the federal government's handling of the case over decades. It urges the Justice Department to reinterview key witnesses and criticizes the Trump administration's release of Epstein records. Democrats, who will run the committee in January, say their inquiry is just starting.
stories.why_it_matters: The report puts on the record that survivors say federal investigators never questioned them, and it sets up further investigations, including of banks, once Democrats take over committees in January.
stories.background: Jeffrey Epstein was a convicted sex offender whose associates included many powerful people. Public pressure to release government files on him led Congress to pass, and President Trump to sign, the Epstein Files Transparency Act nearly a year ago. The House Oversight Committee, chaired by Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.), interviewed many of Epstein's associates. In September Comer introduced a bill aimed at tactics used to silence victims, saying the government had failed them.

The committee called on the Justice Department to reinterview key witnesses.
The report criticizes the Trump administration over its release of Epstein records, the AP reported.

A Politico poll found more voters want Democrats to pursue an affordability agenda than to keep investigating Epstein.
In September, Comer unveiled legislation he said would close human-trafficking loopholes exposed by the Epstein case.

stories.headline: Kennedy family members ask court to block Trump's arch near Arlington Cemetery
stories.summary: Nine members of the Kennedy family asked a federal judge in Washington to block construction of President Trump's planned 250-foot arch near Arlington National Cemetery. They argue it would cast a shadow over family graves and disrupt the view from John F. Kennedy's eternal flame. The filing joins an existing lawsuit as Trump visits the cemetery for Veterans Day.
stories.why_it_matters: The case is one of several testing whether the president can build a large monument on federal land near a national cemetery without approval from Congress or full environmental review.
stories.background: President Trump has proposed a roughly 250-foot triumphal arch in the Washington area, near Arlington National Cemetery, where President John F. Kennedy and other Kennedy family members are buried. Earlier this year, Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian sued to stop it, saying Congress had not approved it. Arlington County, Virginia, also sued, arguing the administration skipped required environmental reviews. The Kennedy relatives are asking to join one of these existing cases.

stories.headline: Democrats lead narrowly as Mississippi and Alaska Senate counts near the end
stories.summary: Ballot deadlines passed Tuesday in Mississippi, where Democrat Scott Colom holds a narrow lead over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola's lead over Sen. Dan Sullivan grew to about 2,500 votes, and a judge is weighing a lawsuit from her campaign over absentee ballots. They are the last two Senate races not yet called.
stories.why_it_matters: The two races will decide how large the new Democratic Senate majority is, which affects how easily it can pass bills and confirm or block nominees.
stories.background: Democrats won control of the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms, but races in Mississippi and Alaska remain too close to call. Mississippi rarely has close statewide races, and a large number of absentee and provisional ballots is still being processed. In Alaska, counting of absentee ballots continues; earlier this month a federal judge dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit that sought to delay certification of the state's Senate race and separate certain ballots.

stories.headline: California voters reject one-time tax on billionaires' wealth
stories.summary: California voters rejected Proposition 40, which would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of residents worth more than $1 billion. The measure split Democrats and drew record opposition spending, much of it from the tech industry. Supporters had seen it as a model for wealth taxes elsewhere.
stories.why_it_matters: The result shows that even in a strongly Democratic year and state, voters turned down a direct tax on the very rich, which is likely to shape whether other states or Congress try similar taxes.
stories.background: A wealth tax charges people on the value of what they own, such as company shares, rather than only on income. Prop 40 would have charged billionaires 5% once, on most of their wealth. Major tech figures funded a large campaign against it, while some Democrats and progressives backed it. The vote took place in the Nov. 3 election, in which Democrats won control of Congress.

stories.headline: US charges three over Iran-linked plots as aircraft leave a second UK base and Bessent moves to a military base
stories.summary: The Justice Department unsealed an indictment charging three men it describes as Iranian operatives with plotting a string of attacks, including the September incident at Britain's RAF Fairford air base. A day earlier, the US Air Force moved aircraft out of RAF Mildenhall in England over what a US official called a threat, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has moved from his Washington-area home to a military base after Iranian threats against his life, according to the New York Times and Reuters sources.
stories.why_it_matters: The cases show the US-Iran conflict reaching into Britain and the US itself, with prosecutors alleging plots against Jewish communities as well as military sites. Iran has denied plotting attacks on officials and people on US soil.
stories.background: The US has been at war with Iran this year, and American bombers flew missions against Iran from RAF Fairford in England. After a security scare near Fairford in late September, the US withdrew all its bombers from that base in early October. Since August, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has led an economic pressure campaign aimed at cutting off money to Iran's Revolutionary Guard. One of the men now charged, Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, was already in US custody after being charged in May with supporting terrorist groups.

facts.text: The US Justice Department on Tuesday announced charges against three men it called Iranian operatives: Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani.
Prosecutors allege the men helped plan and direct the September incident at RAF Fairford, a British base that housed US troops and aircraft.
US authorities allege a campaign of nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks targeting Jewish communities in Europe and the US.
Prosecutors say al-Saadi, a leader of an Iranian-backed militia, helped direct the Fairford plot from a jail in New York by passing along coded messages.
Fox News reported that the indictment alleges the suspects used vans loaded with fuel to target Fairford.
Al-Saadi was transferred to FBI custody and brought to New York in May, when he was first indicted on terrorism-related charges.
The US Air Force moved refueling tankers and other aircraft out of RAF Mildenhall in eastern England on Monday because of a threat, a US official said.
Fox News reported that 13 aircraft left Mildenhall and that the reported Iran-linked threat raised the base to the second-highest military alert level.
Mildenhall is the second UK base the US has pulled aircraft from; all US bombers left RAF Fairford in early October after the September incident.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent moved from his Washington-area home to a military base after Iranian threats against his life, the New York Times first reported and two people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
The New York Times said Bessent is the latest Trump administration official to leave his home over security concerns.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said major combat operations against Iran are no longer needed because US economic pressure is doing enough damage.
Iran's top security official said no talks are under way with the US, and Iran has said the US must meet seven conditions before the Strait of Hormuz reopens.

stories.headline: US Army soldier in a NATO unit arrested in Britain on suspicion of spying for Russia
stories.summary: British counterterrorism police arrested a 41-year-old US Army soldier near Gloucester on suspicion of espionage linked to Russia, in an investigation run jointly with the FBI and US military intelligence. The man, who has not been named, is being held and questioned in London under the UK's National Security Act while police decide on charges.
stories.why_it_matters: A US official said the suspect served at the headquarters of a NATO rapid-response command, so any leak could touch on how the alliance plans to defend Europe.
stories.background: Britain's National Security Act sets out offences for helping foreign intelligence services. Russia's war in Ukraine has led to several espionage cases in Europe. Imjin Barracks near Gloucester is home to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, a command that can quickly deploy forces in a crisis. The arrest came the same day Russia and Ukraine opened US-mediated peace talks in Abu Dhabi.

The investigation was carried out jointly with the FBI and US military intelligence, and the man was held pending possible charges.

stories.headline: Russia and Ukraine hold first US-mediated talks in nine months in Abu Dhabi
stories.summary: Russian and Ukrainian negotiators met with US mediators in Abu Dhabi for two days, their first three-way talks since February. The first session ran nearly four hours. Russian state media said the second day ended in under two hours, and Ukraine planned a separate meeting with European partners afterward. Both sides kept up strikes while the talks went on, including a Ukrainian drone attack that set fire to Russia's Ust-Luga port.
stories.why_it_matters: The war has run for more than four and a half years. Any progress toward ending it would affect energy and grain supplies, European security, and the millions of people living near the front.
stories.background: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine is now about four and a half years old. The US held three rounds of three-way talks early this year without a breakthrough, then the talks were suspended after the war with Iran began. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner lead the mediation. Ukraine's delegation is headed by Rustem Umerov, who leads its foreign intelligence service. The main sticking point remains the security guarantees Ukraine wants against a future attack, which Russia opposes.

facts.text: Russia and Ukraine held nearly four hours of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday.
It was the first three-way meeting since February; talks had been suspended after the war with Iran began.
Ukraine said the first day covered humanitarian and de-escalation steps.
US envoy Steve Witkoff had said the talks would cover post-war security agreements, de-escalation, humanitarian measures and ending the war.
Ukrainian negotiator Rustem Umerov said the second day would start in the three-way format, followed by a separate meeting with European partners.
Russian state media said the second day ended after less than two hours.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said security guarantees for Ukraine must also be acceptable to Russia.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was 'happy' with the approach of the US envoys.
The New York Times reported that a cease-fire would not be on the table.
Russia struck Ukraine's power grid as the talks opened.
A drone attack set off a fire at Russia's Baltic Sea port of Ust-Luga, a major export hub for energy and grain, the regional governor said.
Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia issued, then withdrew, alerts urging people to shelter from unidentified drones entering from Russia or Belarus.

stories.headline: Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 11,000 confirmed cases
stories.summary: The number of confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo has passed 11,000, government data showed Tuesday, in what the Associated Press calls the country's deadliest outbreak. The UN migration agency urged wider surveillance after finding dozens of cases along travel routes, while neighbouring Kenya discharged its last Ebola patient.
stories.why_it_matters: Ebola spreads through contact with the sick, and cases found on travel routes show how it can cross borders. Coverage came from center and left-leaning outlets; no right-leaning outlet in the bundle covered it.
stories.background: Ebola is a severe and often fatal viral disease. This outbreak began in Ituri province in eastern Congo, where the WHO was alerted in early May to an unknown, deadly illness. It was later identified as the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no proven treatment. Armed conflict and a weak health system in eastern Congo have made it hard to contain, and cases have spread to neighbouring countries.

facts.text: Confirmed Ebola cases in Congo passed 11,000, according to government data released Tuesday.
The Associated Press describes it as Congo's deadliest Ebola outbreak.
The outbreak was declared in mid-May, and Congolese authorities have struggled to contain it amid conflict and a health system crisis.
The WHO was alerted in early May to an unknown, high-mortality illness in Ituri province, later linked to the Bundibugyo virus.
The International Organization for Migration said 71 confirmed cases have been detected along transit routes and urged surveillance beyond formal border crossings.
Kenya discharged its last Ebola patient, starting a 42-day countdown to being declared Ebola-free.

stories.headline: Israel's new parliament is sworn in as Eisenkot's bloc moves to undo Netanyahu policies
stories.summary: Israel's 26th Knesset was sworn in Tuesday, with lawmakers opposed to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu holding a majority. Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who has the mandate to form a government, has not yet built a coalition, but his bloc filed bills on its first day to set up a state inquiry into the October 7 attack, limit prime ministers' terms and repeal Netanyahu's judicial overhaul.
stories.why_it_matters: If Eisenkot forms a government, it would end Netanyahu's time in office and could change Israel's policy on the courts, military service and the wars it has fought since 2023. Coverage came from center and left-leaning outlets; no right-leaning outlet in the bundle covered it.
stories.background: Netanyahu has been prime minister through the war years and backed an overhaul of the judiciary that his rivals now want repealed. In last month's election his rivals won more seats, and President Isaac Herzog chose Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, to try to form a government after 67 lawmakers backed him. Eisenkot has a limited time to put together a coalition of at least 61 of the Knesset's 120 seats; if he fails, Netanyahu could get a chance. A key dispute with possible ultra-Orthodox partners is whether their community should be exempt from military service.

facts.text: The 120 members of Israel's 26th Knesset were sworn in on Tuesday.

Eisenkot has not yet formed a coalition, and Netanyahu would get a chance if he fails.
On the first day, Eisenkot's bloc submitted bills to create a state inquiry into October 7, limit prime ministers' terms and repeal the judicial overhaul.
More than 61 lawmakers signed a demand to vote on replacing Knesset Speaker Ohana, and Ohana said the vote would be held next Tuesday.
Herzog, opening the session, called for an investigation of October 7 and urged all sides to avoid another election.
Eisenkot said he would not back down on military service for all, while potential ultra-Orthodox partners in United Torah Judaism insist on draft exemptions.
Eisenkot called Netanyahu's speech 'hate-filled' and said it left him more certain Netanyahu is unfit for office.

stories.headline: Spain holds its first general strike in 14 years over housing costs
stories.summary: Workers across Spain went on strike Wednesday in the country's first general strike in 14 years, demanding that the government address soaring rents and low wages. The strike, called by the main unions, disrupted transport and public services less than three weeks before a November 29 snap election.
stories.why_it_matters: Housing costs are squeezing renters across Spain and much of Europe, and the issue is now central to an election whose result could shift Spanish politics. Coverage came from center and left-leaning outlets; no right-leaning outlet in the bundle covered it.
stories.background: Rents in Spain have risen steeply in recent years, and housing has become the country's top political issue. Spain's two biggest unions, UGT and CCOO, called the 24-hour strike in October. They are demanding rent limits, more public housing and pay rises. The strike comes ahead of a snap national election on November 29.

Spain holds a snap national election on November 29, and housing is the main issue in the campaign.

stories.headline: Bukele says Salvadoran troops destroyed a Haitian gang headquarters
stories.summary: El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele said his military destroyed the headquarters of Haiti's 400 Mawozo gang, part of an offensive by about 2,500 Salvadoran troops in Haiti. The Dominican Republic's president said his government is giving logistics and intelligence support, while Axios reported that US State Department officials have privately raised objections.
stories.why_it_matters: Gang violence has displaced large numbers of Haitians and cut off food and aid. A foreign military campaign could change conditions there, and it also raises questions about civilian safety and oversight.
stories.background: Armed gangs control much of Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince, and international security missions have struggled to restore order. Bukele became known for a crackdown on gangs in El Salvador that critics say involved mass detentions and rights abuses. He sent special forces to Haiti in October after Salvadoran personnel were seized in an attack, then expanded the deployment. Haiti's transitional government backs the mission, and the UN has said it is separate from the existing international force.

facts.text: Bukele said the Salvadoran military destroyed the headquarters of the 400 Mawozo gang.

stories.headline: Malaysia's former leader Najib Razak leaves prison for house arrest
stories.summary: Former Malaysian Prime Minister Najib Razak was moved from prison to house arrest to serve the rest of his corruption sentence after a court cleared the final hurdle for the transfer. DW reported that a minister resigned in protest and that Najib still faces a separate 15-year prison sentence.
stories.why_it_matters: The 1MDB scandal is one of the largest corruption cases in the world, and how Malaysia treats Najib is seen as a test of whether powerful people face the same rules as others.
stories.background: 1MDB was a Malaysian state investment fund at the center of a multibillion-dollar looting scandal. Najib, a former prime minister, was convicted of corruption linked to the fund and has been in prison since August 2022, when his conviction was upheld. A royal pardon process cut his sentence and later allowed him to serve the remainder at home. He was later given a separate sentence in another 1MDB-related case.

stories.headline: Nvidia faces FBI scrutiny, a shareholder suit and calls in Congress for probes over CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy
stories.summary: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence reportedly identified as a Chinese spy. President Trump said the FBI is looking into it, Nvidia hired the law firm Wachtell Lipton to run an internal investigation, shareholders sued, and lawmakers from both parties called for inquiries. Nvidia shares fell sharply on Monday and Tuesday and were reported up about 5% on Wednesday as investors look toward the company's earnings.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is one of the largest companies in the stock market, so its swings move the retirement and index funds many people hold, and the scandal is adding momentum to proposed limits on selling U.S. AI chips abroad.
stories.background: Nvidia makes the chips that power most artificial-intelligence systems, and Jensen Huang is its co-founder and chief executive. Huang has been one of the most prominent voices urging Washington to ease export controls on selling advanced chips to China. Over the weekend he acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a former Shanghai banker turned tech executive at Megaspeed, a company under U.S. investigation over alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips into China, which it denies. Nvidia's board opened an investigation and said it still has confidence in Huang, while Trump has publicly defended him.

facts.text: Huang has admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence has identified as suspected of spying for China, according to reporting by CBS, the BBC and CNBC.

Megaspeed is under U.S. investigation over alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips into China, which it denies, DW reported.
Trump said the FBI is investigating the affair, and that Huang told him he had no idea she was a spy.

Nvidia's board said a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, would oversee an investigation, and that it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.
Trump has publicly defended Huang, calling him an "honorable guy."
Nvidia hired Wachtell Lipton to lead the internal inquiry, headed by partner Joon H. Kim, a former acting U.S. attorney in Manhattan.
Nvidia and Huang face a shareholder lawsuit filed in California alleging investors were misled about the affair.
Republicans and Democrats have both called for investigations into whether national security was compromised, but differ on whether the Trump administration is at fault, The Hill reported.
The senior Republican on the Senate Banking Committee called on Huang to resign, Reuters reported.
Lawmakers are pushing new rules on chip sales to China, and the scandal has added momentum to three bills that would restrict chip exports.
A blacklisted Chinese university linked to the military bought Nvidia H200 chips despite U.S. export rules, according to procurement records reported by Reuters.
Nvidia shares fell more than 4% on Monday, erasing roughly $200 billion in market value, CBS reported.

The stock was down 5.9% at $168.12 on Tuesday, with nearly $450 billion lost over two days, the New York Post reported, and Microsoft passed Nvidia in market value for the first time since June 2025, per Reuters.
Nvidia shares were up about 5% on Wednesday as investors weighed whether the affair will affect the business ahead of earnings, CNBC reported.
Major Nvidia investors publicly backed Huang while privately expressing disappointment, Axios reported.

stories.headline: Hotter-than-expected October inflation raises bets on a December Fed rate hike
stories.summary: Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, less than in September but more than economists expected, with food, energy and housing costs all rising. Several Federal Reserve officials signaled support for raising interest rates again, traders priced in a December hike, short-term Treasury yields jumped and the dollar rose. U.S. stocks slipped on Tuesday; the bond market is closed Wednesday for Veterans Day.
stories.why_it_matters: Higher interest rates make mortgages, car loans and credit-card balances more expensive, while inflation running near 4% means paychecks buy less.
stories.background: The Consumer Price Index, published monthly by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, tracks what households pay for a basket of goods and services. Prices have been pushed up this year in part by an energy shock tied to the U.S.-Iran war. The Federal Reserve fights inflation by raising its benchmark interest rate, which makes borrowing costlier and cools spending. Its next rate decision is at the Dec. 9 meeting, and officials including Christopher Waller have been signaling more hikes.

facts.text: The consumer price index rose 0.4% from September to October, slightly above forecasts.

Axios reported that October was the third straight month of hotter-than-expected inflation.
PBS NewsHour said the country appears headed for annual inflation of about 4% this year.
Fed official Christopher Waller plans to support at least a quarter-point rate hike in December, Reuters reported.
Fed official Lorie Logan called for two more hikes, possibly in quick succession, and Fed official Anna Paulson called for gradual hikes, according to Reuters.
Traders are betting on near-certain odds of a quarter-point hike at the Fed's Dec. 9 meeting, the New York Post reported.
Two-year Treasury yields jumped the most since 2024 after the report, and the dollar rose to a four-week high.
U.S. stocks slipped on Tuesday following the report.
The Treasury market is closed Wednesday for Veterans Day.

stories.summary: Brent crude fell below $90 a barrel, its lowest since late August, after President Trump said the war with Iran is "effectively over" and pulled back from threats of further strikes. stories.headline: Anthropic targets a trillion-dollar-plus valuation for its IPO, with reports it may go higher
stories.summary: AI company Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, is seeking a valuation of roughly $1.3 trillion to $1.4 trillion in a stock market listing expected next week, according to multiple reports. The Financial Times reported that bankers are preparing to raise the target to $1.5 trillion or more after strong investor demand, and Anthropic opened a retail offering in Australia on Wednesday.
stories.why_it_matters: It would be one of the largest stock listings ever, and investors are treating it as a test of whether the AI boom that has driven stock indexes can continue.
stories.background: Anthropic is an artificial-intelligence company that develops the Claude family of AI models. It filed to go public in the fall, and an amended filing this month added third-quarter results showing revenue of about $17 billion for the quarter. Earlier reports had it aiming for about $2 trillion before investors cooled on AI stocks. Large tech companies including Nvidia and TSMC are investing alongside the listing. stories.headline: Mamdani signs law giving nonprofits first chance to buy distressed buildings
stories.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Tuesday signed the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act (COPA), which gives nonprofit housing groups the first opportunity to buy certain distressed and affordable apartment buildings when they go up for sale. The signing ends a fight of about six years that included a veto by former Mayor Eric Adams. Real estate groups have opposed the measure, while supporters describe it as protection against speculative investors.
stories.why_it_matters: Tenants in rundown or rent-regulated buildings could see more of them pass to nonprofit owners, while landlords selling such buildings face a new step before a sale. Coverage in the ingest came from center and right-leaning outlets; no left-leaning outlet in the bundle covered the signing.
stories.background: COPA requires owners of covered buildings to notify qualified nonprofits before selling, similar to policies in Washington, D.C. and San Francisco, according to industry summaries of the bill. The City Council bill, introduced as Intro 902, went through several rounds of amendments after real estate groups warned it would slow building sales. The landlord group New York Apartment Association testified against it. Brooklyn Paper reports that the bill survived a veto by Mayor Eric Adams and months of negotiation before reaching Mamdani, a democratic socialist who took office in January 2026.

markets.summary: Stocks fell on Tuesday after the government reported that consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, more than economists had forecast. Faster inflation makes it more likely the Federal Reserve will raise its benchmark interest rate in December, and that expectation pushed up Treasury yields, the interest rate the government pays to borrow, as well as the dollar, Reuters and the Financial Times reported. The Nasdaq, heavy with technology companies, fell more than the broader market as Nvidia's shares kept sliding amid the scandal around its chief executive. The mood improved after the close: cloud-computing company CoreWeave reported results that eased fears of a slowdown in AI spending, and stock futures and European chip stocks rose early Wednesday, according to Reuters and CNBC. concept.explanation: An IPO is when a privately owned company first sells shares to the public on a stock exchange, as AI company Anthropic is preparing to do at a valuation reported to be above $1 trillion. Investment banks gauge how many shares investors want and at what price, so strong demand can push the valuation up while a falling market can shrink or delay the sale. You can be affected even without buying shares directly, because large newly listed companies are eventually added to stock indexes that many retirement funds track. Big IPOs are also watched as a sign of how willing investors are to take on risk.
